client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother died six months ago. Every time my friends invite me out, I go sometimes, but I just feel completely hollow inside, like I'm watching everyone else laugh and have fun through a glass wall. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, honestly, because it's not like you can just fix grief.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — that image of watching life through a glass wall really captures something deep about grief, that sense of being present but somehow unreachable. I notice you came here even while doubting it will help, and I'm curious about that part of you that showed up anyway — what do you think brought you here today? And as you speak, there's something in your voice that feels even quieter and more distant than your words alone — I just want to gently check in: how are you actually doing right now, in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess what brought me here is that I'm just... exhausted from pretending I'm okay when I'm not. There's this part of me that thought maybe if I said it out loud to someone, even a stranger, it might feel less like I'm suffocating under it. But right now, in this moment, I feel kind of exposed and honestly a little stupid for thinking talking could fix the fact that my mom died six months ago and nothing feels real anymore.
therapist: First, I want to gently hold something you just said — you mentioned your brother earlier, and now your mom; it sounds like you've lost two people who mattered deeply to you, and I don't want to rush past that without acknowledging what an enormous weight that is to carry. There's nothing stupid about reaching out when you're suffocating — in fact, it takes a quiet kind of courage to say out loud "I'm not okay" when you've been holding it together for everyone else. Can you tell me a little more about what "nothing feels real" has been like for you day to day?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It's weird because I'll be doing something completely ordinary, like making coffee or driving to work, and it just hits me that my brother is gone and my mom is gone and I'm just... still here, going through the motions. Like I'm watching myself from the outside, if that makes any sense. Some days I genuinely can't tell if I'm functioning or just really good at pretending to.
therapist: What you're describing — that sense of watching yourself from the outside, going through the motions — is actually a really recognized response to profound loss, a kind of protective distance your mind creates when the pain is almost too much to hold directly. And yet even as you describe it in measured words, there's something in your voice that sounds even more drained and far away than what you're saying, like the exhaustion runs deeper than you might even be letting yourself fully feel right now. I'm wondering — when you're in those ordinary moments, like making coffee, and it hits you, what do you usually do with that feeling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I usually just... push through it, I guess. Like I'll focus really hard on the task, counting the scoops of coffee or watching the water boil, just to give my brain something concrete to hold onto. But then I feel guilty about that too, like I'm somehow disrespecting his memory by not letting myself actually feel it.
therapist: That guilt you're describing is such a common and painful trap in grief — your mind has found a way to survive the unsurvivable, and then turns around and punishes you for it. Focusing on the coffee scoops isn't disrespecting your brother or your mom; it's actually you finding a way to keep breathing when the weight gets unbearable. I'm curious — whose voice is that, the one telling you that pushing through means you're doing grief wrong?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I never really thought about it that way — like whose voice it actually is. I think... it might be my mom's, honestly, even though she's never said it directly to me. She just always seemed so openly devastated all the time, and I guess I started to feel like if I wasn't falling apart the same way she was, I must not have loved him as much.
therapist: That's such a profound realization — you've been measuring your love for your brother against someone else's way of grieving, as if there's only one right way to show how much he mattered to you. And as you say that, your voice sounds very small and quiet, like this is something tender and fragile you're only just allowing yourself to look at. I want to ask gently — what do *you* think it means that you've found ways to keep going, even when it's hard?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I think... it probably means I'm stronger than I give myself credit for, but saying that out loud feels almost wrong, like I'm betraying him somehow. Like if I admit I've been coping, it means his loss didn't hit me as hard as it should have. I don't know how to hold both things at once — that I loved him deeply and that I've somehow kept moving forward.
therapist: What you just said — that you're stronger than you give yourself credit for — I want you to sit with that for a moment, because it's true, and you deserve to let it be true. Loving someone deeply and continuing to live aren't opposites; in fact, keeping going in the face of this kind of loss *is* how love sometimes looks from the inside. I wonder if part of what makes it feel like a betrayal is that moving forward feels like moving away from him — is that part of what's underneath this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think that's... actually pretty close to what it feels like. Like if I stop grieving so hard, or if I have a good day, it means he's getting further away somehow, like the distance between us is growing. And I don't know how to want to close that distance without feeling like I'm doing something wrong.
therapist: What you're describing is one of the most painful paradoxes of grief — that staying close to him feels like it requires staying close to the pain, as if the hurt is the last thread connecting you. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if carrying him forward with you, into good days and ordinary moments, is actually a way of keeping him near rather than leaving him behind? What do you think he would want for you, if he could see you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it almost feels too easy, like a nice way to package something that's actually just loss. When I try to imagine what he'd want for me, I honestly don't know if I can trust that thought, because it feels like I'm just putting words in his mouth to make myself feel better. And if I let myself have good days, it's like I'm admitting that life goes on without him, and I'm not sure I'm ready to admit that yet.
therapist: You're not ready to admit that yet — and that's okay, you don't have to be. There's something really honest and important in what you just said, that "life goes on without him" feels like a fact you're not ready to make peace with, and I don't want to rush you past that with a reframe that feels too neat. Can we just sit with that for a moment — what does it feel like to say out loud that you're not ready yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Saying it out loud... it feels like admitting defeat somehow, like I'm confirming that he really is gone and that the world just kept spinning anyway, which is almost cruel when I think about it. There's this weird guilt too, like if I accept it, I'm betraying him or saying his absence doesn't matter. I don't know, it's heavy just sitting here with that thought.
therapist: The weight in your voice as you say that is palpable — and I want to gently push back on one thing: accepting that he's gone isn't the same as saying his absence doesn't matter, and it isn't defeat. What strikes me is that you're carrying this almost impossible equation in your heart, where acceptance equals erasure, but I wonder if his absence mattering and life continuing could somehow both be true at the same time. What would it mean for you if those two things didn't have to cancel each other out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but it feels almost too neat, like a way of making peace with something that shouldn't have happened. If I let life just... continue, it feels like I'm admitting that the world can function fine without him in it, and that thought makes me feel sick. I don't know how to hold both of those things without one of them swallowing the other.
therapist: That feeling of sickness — that's not a thinking problem, that's grief telling the truth about how much he mattered, and I don't want to talk you out of that. Your voice sounds very small and quiet right now, like you're holding something almost too heavy to say, and I just want you to know you don't have to resolve this today — you don't have to find a way to hold both things neatly. What would it feel like to just let yourself not have an answer for a little while?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
